```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  echo = FALSE,
  message = FALSE,
  warning = FALSE,
  fig.align = "center",
  fig.pos = "H",
  out.extra = "",
  dev = "png",
  dpi = 200
)

library(ggplot2)
library(patchwork)

theme_set(
  theme_minimal(base_size = 10) + theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank())
)

## Every figure carries this, so a figure lifted out of the document still says what it is.
SIM_NOTE <- "SIMULATED DATA - not real results"
sim_theme <- theme(
  plot.caption = element_text(
    colour = "#B2182B",
    face = "bold",
    size = 9,
    hjust = 1
  )
)
sim_caption <- function() list(labs(caption = SIM_NOTE), sim_theme)
sim_annotation <- function() {
  patchwork::plot_annotation(caption = SIM_NOTE, theme = sim_theme)
}

## Palettes. Connectivity classes use the pipeline's fixed colours (`R/connectivity_categories.R`),
## so these figures read the same as the district maps.
CONN_CLASSES <- c("Impeded", "Diffuse", "Intensified", "Channelized")
CONN_COLOURS <- c(
  Impeded = "#B2182B",
  Diffuse = "#F7F7F7",
  Intensified = "#92C5DE",
  Channelized = "#2166AC"
)
SERAL_CLASSES <- c("Early", "Mid", "Mature", "Old")
SERAL_COLOURS <- c(
  Early = "#A1D99B",
  Mid = "#74C476",
  Mature = "#31A354",
  Old = "#00441B"
)
AGENTS <- c("None", "Harvest", "Fire", "Beetle")
AGENT_COLOURS <- c(
  None = "#BDBDBD",
  Harvest = "#0072B2",
  Fire = "#D55E00",
  Beetle = "#009E73"
)
ZONE_COLOURS <- c("Zone A" = "#0072B2", "Zone B" = "#D55E00")

## Changes in cumulative current are analysed as log2 ratios; label them as percent changes.
pct_lab <- function(b) ifelse(abs(b) < 1e-9, "0%", sprintf("%+.0f%%", 100 * (2^b - 1)))
PCT_BREAKS <- log2(c(0.25, 0.5, 0.8, 1, 1.25, 2, 4))
diverging <- function(
  lim,
  name,
  labels = ggplot2::waiver(),
  breaks = ggplot2::waiver()
) {
  scale_fill_gradient2(
    low = "#B2182B",
    mid = "#F7F7F7",
    high = "#2166AC",
    midpoint = 0,
    limits = c(-lim, lim),
    oob = scales::squish,
    name = name,
    labels = labels,
    breaks = breaks,
    na.value = "grey85",
    guide = guide_colourbar(barheight = grid::unit(3, "cm"))
  )
}
```

```{r simulate}
## A simulated landscape --------------------------------------------------------------------------
##
## Nothing here is fitted to the study area. The aim is a landscape whose connectivity surfaces
## behave qualitatively like Omniscape outputs, so each method has something to show.

set.seed(20261029)

NR <- 120L
NC <- 120L
RES <- 90
EPOCHS <- seq(1995L, 2025L, by = 5L)

template <- terra::rast(
  nrows = NR,
  ncols = NC,
  xmin = 0,
  xmax = NC * RES,
  ymin = 0,
  ymax = NR * RES,
  crs = "EPSG:3005"
)

## smoothed Gaussian noise, rescaled to mean 0 and sd 1
grf <- function(sigma_cells) {
  r <- template
  terra::values(r) <- stats::rnorm(terra::ncell(r))
  w <- terra::focalMat(r, sigma_cells * RES, type = "Gauss")
  r <- terra::focal(r, w, fun = "sum", na.rm = TRUE)
  v <- terra::values(r, mat = FALSE)
  terra::values(r) <- (v - mean(v)) / stats::sd(v)
  r
}

## Gaussian-weighted sum over a neighbourhood of `sigma_cells`
smooth <- function(v, sigma_cells) {
  r <- template
  terra::values(r) <- v
  w <- terra::focalMat(r, sigma_cells * RES, "Gauss")
  terra::values(terra::focal(r, w, fun = "sum", na.rm = TRUE), mat = FALSE)
}

age <- round(stats::pnorm(terra::values(grf(5), mat = FALSE)) * 260)
pine <- terra::values(grf(8), mat = FALSE) > 0.2
xy <- terra::xyFromCell(template, seq_len(terra::ncell(template)))
zone <- ifelse(xy[, 1] + 0.3 * xy[, 2] < 0.6 * NC * RES, "Zone A", "Zone B")

## Cells inside a rectangle centred on `cell`
block_cells <- function(cell, w, h) {
  rc <- terra::rowColFromCell(template, cell)
  rows <- pmin(pmax(rc[1] + seq(-h %/% 2, h %/% 2), 1), NR)
  cols <- pmin(pmax(rc[2] + seq(-w %/% 2, w %/% 2), 1), NC)
  terra::cellFromRowCol(
    template,
    rep(rows, each = length(cols)),
    rep(cols, length(rows))
  )
}

## Disturbance in each 5-year interval: harvest blocks throughout, a beetle outbreak peaking
## 2000-2010 in pine-leading stands, and a large fire in 2015-2020.
n_blocks <- c(10, 12, 16, 18, 14, 10)
beetle_rate <- c(0.03, 0.20, 0.25, 0.05, 0.01, 0.00)
fire_events <- list(
  NULL,
  list(c(25, 95), 7),
  NULL,
  NULL,
  list(c(85, 30), 17),
  NULL
)

ages <- list(age)
agents <- list()
for (k in seq_along(n_blocks)) {
  a <- rep("None", length(age))

  ## beetle: clustered mortality in older pine
  if (beetle_rate[k] > 0) {
    clump <- terra::values(grf(2), mat = FALSE)
    hit <- pine & age >= 60 & clump > stats::qnorm(1 - beetle_rate[k])
    a[hit] <- "Beetle"
  }

  ## fire: an irregular patch around a centre
  if (!is.null(fire_events[[k]])) {
    ctr <- fire_events[[k]][[1]] * RES
    rad <- fire_events[[k]][[2]] * RES
    d <- sqrt((xy[, 1] - ctr[1])^2 + (xy[, 2] - ctr[2])^2)
    edge <- terra::values(grf(3), mat = FALSE)
    a[d < rad * (1 + 0.35 * edge)] <- "Fire"
  }

  ## harvest last, so salvage of beetle-killed stands counts as harvest
  eligible <- which(age >= 80)
  for (b in seq_len(n_blocks[k])) {
    centre <- eligible[sample.int(length(eligible), 1)]
    a[block_cells(centre, sample(3:9, 1), sample(3:9, 1))] <- "Harvest"
  }

  age <- age + 5
  age[a != "None"] <- sample(0:4, sum(a != "None"), replace = TRUE)
  ages[[k + 1]] <- age
  agents[[k]] <- a
}
names(ages) <- EPOCHS
names(agents) <- paste(head(EPOCHS, -1), EPOCHS[-1], sep = "-")

seral_of <- function(age) {
  factor(
    cut(age, c(-Inf, 40, 80, 140, Inf), right = FALSE, labels = SERAL_CLASSES),
    levels = SERAL_CLASSES
  )
}

## Stand-ins for Omniscape's three outputs.
##
## Conductance (1 / resistance) rises with stand age; source strength is on the same 0-1 scale at
## every snapshot, as the pipeline's source weights are, and is high only in old forest.
conductance <- function(age) 0.08 + 0.92 * (pmin(age, 160) / 160)^1.5
source_wt <- function(age) 0.02 + 0.98 * (pmin(age, 200) / 200)^2

## Normalized current: a cell's conductance relative to its neighbourhood. Old forest surrounded
## by young stands carries more than its share (channelized); young stands within an old-forest
## matrix carry less (impeded).
norm_current <- function(age) {
  c0 <- conductance(age)
  f <- smooth((c0 / smooth(c0, 6))^0.75, 1)
  pmin(pmax(f * exp(stats::rnorm(length(f), 0, 0.04)), 0.05), 5)
}
flow <- lapply(ages, norm_current)

## Flow potential: what the sources within the moving window would deliver with no resistance.
potential <- lapply(ages, function(a) smooth(source_wt(a), 8))

## Cumulative current, so that cumulative / potential is the normalized current above: the same
## relationship Omniscape's three outputs have.
cumcur <- Map(`*`, flow, potential)
lcum <- lapply(cumcur, log2)

classify <- function(f) {
  factor(
    cut(f, c(-Inf, 0.7, 1.3, 1.7, Inf), labels = CONN_CLASSES, right = TRUE),
    levels = CONN_CLASSES
  )
}
conn <- lapply(flow, classify)

## Reporting areas: the two zones above stand in for BEC zones; 16 landscape units are the
## Voronoi cells of random seeds. Drawn last, so they do not change the landscape above.
seeds <- cbind(stats::runif(16, 0, NC * RES), stats::runif(16, 0, NR * RES))
d2 <- outer(xy[, 1], seeds[, 1], "-")^2 + outer(xy[, 2], seeds[, 2], "-")^2
lu <- sprintf("LU %02d", max.col(-d2))
lu_zone <- tapply(zone, lu, function(z) names(which.max(table(z))))

## long form, one row per cell per epoch
cells <- dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(seq_along(EPOCHS), function(i) {
  data.frame(
    cell = seq_along(ages[[i]]),
    x = xy[, 1],
    y = xy[, 2],
    zone = zone,
    lu = lu,
    epoch = EPOCHS[i],
    age = ages[[i]],
    seral = seral_of(ages[[i]]),
    flow = flow[[i]],
    lcum = lcum[[i]],
    class = conn[[i]]
  )
}))
```

::: {.callout-important}
## Every figure in this document uses simulated data

The maps, plots and numbers below come from a made-up 120 x 120-cell landscape (90 m cells, about 10.8 x 10.8 km) with invented disturbance.
They show what each summary would look like and how it reads.
They say nothing about Cariboo-Chilcotin, 100 Mile House, or Quesnel.
:::

# Purpose

The historical series will give us Omniscape connectivity surfaces and forest patch layers for each of seven snapshots, 1995 to 2025 at five-year steps.
This document lays out candidate ways to summarize how connectivity changed across those snapshots, so we can choose which to carry forward before the real runs finish.
Each method is shown on simulated data, with what it answers, what it cannot answer, and the choices it needs from us.

There are two families:

1. Methods on the Omniscape current surfaces (@sec-lee to @sec-transitions).
   @sec-layer first sets out which of Omniscape's outputs each method should use.
2. Methods on patch layers -- old and mature forest, or other definitions -- using standard landscape pattern metrics (@sec-fragstats).

The two are complementary.
The Omniscape surfaces describe how movement is routed across the whole landscape, including the matrix.
Patch metrics describe habitat (or whatever the patches are taken to be) without any model of movement.
@sec-areas covers summarizing all of them by reporting area.

## The simulated landscape

@fig-overview shows the simulated landscape at the start and end of the series.
Stand age starts as a smooth random surface and advances five years per step.
Three disturbance agents reset age to zero: harvest blocks in every interval, a beetle outbreak in pine-leading stands peaking in 2000--2010, and two fires, a small one in 2000--2005 and a large one in 2015--2020.

The current surfaces are not Omniscape runs.
They are stand-ins built to have the same relationships as Omniscape's outputs: resistance and source strength follow stand age, flow potential is the source strength within a moving window, normalized current is high where a cell conducts better than its neighbourhood, and cumulative current is normalized current times flow potential.
Connectivity classes use the same cut-offs as the real outputs [@Cameron:2022; @McRae:2016]: Impeded at or below 0.7, Diffuse to 1.3, Intensified to 1.7, Channelized above.

```{r map-helpers}
map_theme <- theme(
  axis.text = element_blank(),
  panel.grid = element_blank(),
  legend.key.size = unit(0.3, "cm"),
  legend.text = element_text(size = 7),
  legend.title = element_text(size = 8)
)
map_layer <- function(df, fill, title) {
  ggplot(df, aes(x / 1000, y / 1000, fill = .data[[fill]])) +
    geom_raster() +
    coord_equal(expand = FALSE) +
    labs(x = NULL, y = NULL, title = title) +
    map_theme
}

## who disturbed each cell most recently, by 2025
last_agent <- Reduce(
  function(prev, a) ifelse(a == "None", prev, a),
  agents,
  accumulate = FALSE
)
```

```{r fig-overview}
#| fig-cap: "**Simulated data.** The simulated landscape in 1995 and 2025: seral stage (top), the most recent stand-replacing disturbance by 2025 (top right), and connectivity class from the stand-in for normalized current (bottom)."
#| fig-width: 7.5
#| fig-height: 6.2
d95 <- dplyr::filter(cells, epoch == 1995)
d25 <- dplyr::filter(cells, epoch == 2025)
d25$agent <- factor(last_agent, levels = AGENTS)

seral_scale <- scale_fill_manual(
  values = SERAL_COLOURS,
  name = "Seral stage",
  drop = FALSE
)
conn_scale <- scale_fill_manual(
  values = CONN_COLOURS,
  name = "Connectivity",
  drop = FALSE
)

p <- (map_layer(d95, "seral", "Seral stage, 1995") + seral_scale) +
  (map_layer(d25, "seral", "Seral stage, 2025") + seral_scale) +
  (map_layer(d25, "agent", "Last disturbance, by 2025") +
    scale_fill_manual(values = AGENT_COLOURS, name = "Agent")) +
  (map_layer(d95, "class", "Connectivity, 1995") + conn_scale) +
  (map_layer(d25, "class", "Connectivity, 2025") + conn_scale) +
  patchwork::guide_area() +
  patchwork::plot_layout(ncol = 3, guides = "collect") +
  sim_annotation()
p
```

# Which Omniscape output to compare over time {#sec-layer}

::: {.callout-note}
## Recommendation

Normalized current is the wrong layer for measuring *how much* connectivity changed between snapshots.
Use **cumulative current** for that, and keep normalized current for the connectivity classes (@sec-transitions), where it is the layer the classes are defined on.
:::

Omniscape writes three surfaces:

- **Cumulative current**: the modelled flow through each cell, from all sources within the moving window.
- **Flow potential**: the flow the same sources would produce if every cell had the lowest resistance.
- **Normalized current**: cumulative current divided by flow potential.
  Values above 1 mean flow is being concentrated through a cell; values below 1 mean it is being held back.

Normalized current is built to compare places *within one map*: it removes the effect of how much habitat is nearby, leaving how the landscape routes the flow.
That is what makes it the right basis for the Impeded-to-Channelized classes.

Across snapshots it is a poor measure of change, because its denominator changes too.
Each snapshot in the historical series is run with its own source weights (old forest is the source) and its own resistance, so flow potential is recomputed for each snapshot.
A change in normalized current therefore mixes a change in flow with a change in the yardstick it is measured against.
When old forest is lost, flow potential falls along with the flow, and the ratio can stay level while the amount of movement the model predicts drops substantially.

Cumulative current does not have this problem in our runs.
The source weights are on the same 0--1 scale at every snapshot, and the moving-window radius and all other settings are fixed across snapshots, so a cell's cumulative current can be compared directly between years.
Because it spans orders of magnitude, change in cumulative current is best expressed as a ratio (a percentage change), not a difference.

```{r layer}
layer_means <- data.frame(
  epoch = EPOCHS,
  `Cumulative current` = vapply(cumcur, mean, numeric(1)),
  `Flow potential` = vapply(potential, mean, numeric(1)),
  `Normalized current` = vapply(flow, mean, numeric(1)),
  check.names = FALSE
) |>
  tidyr::pivot_longer(-epoch, names_to = "layer") |>
  dplyr::group_by(layer) |>
  dplyr::mutate(index = 100 * value / value[1]) |>
  dplyr::ungroup()

idx_2025 <- function(l) {
  round(layer_means$index[layer_means$layer == l & layer_means$epoch == 2025])
}
```


In the simulation (@fig-layer), the landscape mean of cumulative current falls to `r idx_2025("Cumulative current")`% of its 1995 value and flow potential to `r idx_2025("Flow potential")`%, while mean normalized current ends at `r idx_2025("Normalized current")`%.
The two change maps also disagree on *where*: normalized current rises around many disturbances, because the remaining forest beside them now carries a larger share of a smaller flow, while cumulative current shows the net loss.

What this means for the methods that follow:

- **Lee's L** (@sec-lee) and **change by disturbance agent** (@sec-agents) use cumulative current, on a log scale.
- **Transitions between classes** (@sec-transitions) use normalized current, because that is what the classes are defined on; read them as changes in how flow is routed, not in how much there is.
- If a normalized measure is wanted for change over time, one option is to divide every snapshot's cumulative current by a *single* reference flow potential (e.g. 2025's), so the denominator stays fixed.
  That keeps the familiar scale, but the result no longer matches the published class definitions, so it should not be classified with them.

```{r fig-layer}
#| fig-cap: "**Simulated data.** Top: landscape means of the three Omniscape outputs, indexed to 1995 = 100. Bottom: change from 1995 to 2025 in normalized current (as a difference) and in cumulative current (as a percentage change)."
#| fig-width: 7.5
#| fig-height: 5.4
p_idx <- ggplot(layer_means, aes(epoch, index, colour = layer)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 100, colour = "grey60") +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.7) +
  geom_point(size = 1.8) +
  scale_colour_manual(
    values = c(
      "Cumulative current" = "#0072B2",
      "Flow potential" = "#009E73",
      "Normalized current" = "#D55E00"
    ),
    name = NULL
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = EPOCHS) +
  labs(x = "Snapshot", y = "Landscape mean (1995 = 100)")

dl <- data.frame(
  x = xy[, 1],
  y = xy[, 2],
  dflow = flow[[7]] - flow[[1]],
  dcum = lcum[[7]] - lcum[[1]]
)
p_dn <- map_layer(dl, "dflow", "Normalized current, change") +
  diverging(stats::quantile(abs(dl$dflow), 0.99), "Difference")
p_dc <- map_layer(dl, "dcum", "Cumulative current, change") +
  diverging(2, "Change", labels = pct_lab, breaks = log2(c(0.25, 0.5, 1, 2, 4)))

p_idx /
  (p_dn | p_dc) +
  patchwork::plot_layout(heights = c(1, 1.5)) +
  sim_annotation()
```

# Lee's L: how similar is the spatial pattern between snapshots? {#sec-lee}

## What it measures

Lee's L [@Lee:2001] is a bivariate measure of spatial association.
It combines Pearson's correlation with Moran's I: before correlating two maps it averages each over a cell's neighbours, so it asks whether *neighbourhoods* that are high on one map are high on the other.
It runs from -1 to 1.
Applied to two snapshots of the same surface, it measures how much the spatial pattern of connectivity persisted.

Lee's L compares patterns, not amounts: an even loss of flow everywhere leaves it unchanged.
It answers a different question from the change in cumulative current in @sec-layer, and the two should be reported together.

A permutation test gives a p-value, but with tens of thousands of autocorrelated cells almost any L is "significant" -- every p-value here is below 0.01.
The useful quantities are the size of L and how it changes through the series.

Lee's L also has a **local** form: one value per cell, whose mean is the global L.
Mapped, it shows where the pattern held (high values) and where it broke (low or negative values: neighbourhoods whose relative flow reversed between the two snapshots).

## Three ways to compare the snapshots

There are three defensible sets of comparisons, each answering a different question.
They are shown below, one figure each, computed on log cumulative current.
Each figure has the global L under two neighbourhood definitions (top) and maps of local L within 360 m (bottom).
We can report one, two or all three.

```{r lee}
nb_queen <- spdep::cell2nb(NR, NC, type = "queen")
nb_wide <- spdep::dnearneigh(xy, 0, 4 * RES)
WIDE <- "Within 4 cells (360 m)"
lw <- list(
  "Adjacent cells (90 m)" = spdep::nb2listw(nb_queen, style = "W"),
  "Within 4 cells (360 m)" = spdep::nb2listw(nb_wide, style = "W")
)

## `cell2nb()` numbers cells column-major from the bottom-left; terra numbers them row-major from
## the top-left. Reorder the values to match the neighbour list.
rc <- terra::rowColFromCell(template, seq_len(terra::ncell(template)))
cell2nb_order <- order(rc[, 2], NR - rc[, 1])
by_scheme <- function(v, scheme) {
  if (grepl("^Adjacent", scheme)) v[cell2nb_order] else v
}

lee_L <- function(x, y, scheme, nsim = 199) {
  t <- spdep::lee.mc(
    by_scheme(x, scheme),
    by_scheme(y, scheme),
    lw[[scheme]],
    nsim = nsim
  )
  c(L = unname(t$statistic), p = t$p.value)
}

## Leave-one-out: each snapshot against the mean of the OTHER six, so the snapshot is not
## correlated against itself.
loo_mean <- function(i) Reduce(`+`, lcum[-i]) / (length(lcum) - 1)

comparisons <- list(
  mean = lapply(seq_along(EPOCHS), function(i) {
    list(
      x = lcum[[i]],
      y = loo_mean(i),
      label = as.character(EPOCHS[i]),
      epoch = EPOCHS[i]
    )
  }),
  consec = lapply(2:length(EPOCHS), function(i) {
    list(
      x = lcum[[i - 1]],
      y = lcum[[i]],
      label = paste(EPOCHS[i - 1], EPOCHS[i], sep = "-"),
      epoch = EPOCHS[i]
    )
  }),
  base = lapply(2:length(EPOCHS), function(i) {
    list(
      x = lcum[[1]],
      y = lcum[[i]],
      label = paste(EPOCHS[1], EPOCHS[i], sep = "-"),
      epoch = EPOCHS[i]
    )
  })
)

lee_global <- dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(names(comparisons), function(cmp) {
  dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(comparisons[[cmp]], function(p) {
    dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(names(lw), function(s) {
      data.frame(
        comparison = cmp,
        scheme = s,
        epoch = p$epoch,
        label = p$label,
        t(lee_L(p$x, p$y, s))
      )
    }))
  }))
}))

lee_local <- dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(names(comparisons), function(cmp) {
  dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(comparisons[[cmp]], function(p) {
    data.frame(
      comparison = cmp,
      label = p$label,
      x = xy[, 1],
      y = xy[, 2],
      localL = spdep::lee(
        p$x,
        p$y,
        lw[[WIDE]],
        n = terra::ncell(template)
      )$localL
    )
  }))
}))
## one colour scale for all three figures; a few extreme cells would otherwise wash the maps out
lim_L <- stats::quantile(abs(lee_local$localL), 0.98)

## global L for inline text
gL <- function(cmp, scheme, lab) {
  sprintf(
    "%.2f",
    lee_global$L[
      lee_global$comparison == cmp &
        lee_global$scheme == scheme &
        lee_global$label == lab
    ]
  )
}
gL_min <- function(cmp, scheme) {
  g <- lee_global[lee_global$comparison == cmp & lee_global$scheme == scheme, ]
  g$label[which.min(g$L)]
}
consec_mean <- function(scheme) {
  sprintf(
    "%.2f",
    mean(lee_global$L[
      lee_global$comparison == "consec" & lee_global$scheme == scheme
    ])
  )
}

lee_figure <- function(cmp, x_title) {
  g <- dplyr::filter(lee_global, comparison == cmp)
  p1 <- ggplot(g, aes(epoch, L, colour = scheme)) +
    geom_line(linewidth = 0.7) +
    geom_point(size = 1.8) +
    scale_colour_manual(
      values = stats::setNames(c("#0072B2", "#D55E00"), names(lw)),
      name = "Neighbours"
    ) +
    scale_x_continuous(breaks = unique(g$epoch), labels = unique(g$label)) +
    labs(x = x_title, y = "Lee's L (global)") +
    theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 30, hjust = 1))

  l <- dplyr::filter(lee_local, comparison == cmp)
  l$label <- factor(l$label, levels = unique(l$label))
  p2 <- ggplot(l, aes(x / 1000, y / 1000, fill = localL)) +
    geom_raster() +
    facet_wrap(~label, ncol = 4) +
    coord_equal(expand = FALSE) +
    diverging(lim_L, "Local L\n(360 m)") +
    labs(x = NULL, y = NULL) +
    map_theme

  p1 / p2 + patchwork::plot_layout(heights = c(1, 1.9)) + sim_annotation()
}
```

### Option A: each snapshot against the rest of the series

The per-cell mean of the other six snapshots is a reference pattern for the period; L for each snapshot says how typical that year's pattern is (@fig-lee-mean).
The snapshot itself is left out of the mean so that it is not partly correlated with itself.
This answers "which years were unusual?", and the local maps show where each year departs from the period's usual pattern.

```{r fig-lee-mean}
#| fig-cap: "**Simulated data.** Option A: Lee's L between each snapshot and the mean of the other six. Top: global L under two neighbourhood definitions. Bottom: local L within 360 m, colour scale capped at the 98th percentile of absolute values across all three options."
#| fig-width: 7.5
#| fig-height: 6.6
lee_figure("mean", "Snapshot")
```

In the simulation the least typical snapshot is `r gL_min("mean", WIDE)` within 360 m (L = `r gL("mean", WIDE, gL_min("mean", WIDE))`), and `r gL_min("mean", names(lw)[1])` with adjacent-cell neighbours.

### Option B: consecutive snapshots

Each snapshot against the one before it (@fig-lee-consec).
This places change in an *interval*, which is what links it to the disturbance record (@sec-agents).
The mean of the six values is a single summary of pattern stability for the whole series: `r consec_mean(names(lw)[1])` with adjacent-cell neighbours and `r consec_mean(WIDE)` within 360 m in the simulation.

```{r fig-lee-consec}
#| fig-cap: "**Simulated data.** Option B: Lee's L between consecutive snapshots, plotted at the later snapshot of each pair. Top: global L. Bottom: local L within 360 m."
#| fig-width: 7.5
#| fig-height: 5.6
lee_figure("consec", "Interval")
```

The lowest value, the interval with the most rearrangement, is `r gL_min("consec", names(lw)[1])` with adjacent-cell neighbours and `r gL_min("consec", WIDE)` within 360 m.

### Option C: each snapshot against 1995

Each snapshot against the first (@fig-lee-base).
This shows cumulative drift: how far the pattern has moved from the start of the record.
It declines more or less steadily by construction, so the interest is in its rate -- where it steepens -- and in the local maps, which accumulate the places where the pattern has broken since 1995.
In the simulation, L between 1995 and 2025 is `r gL("base", WIDE, "1995-2025")` within 360 m.

```{r fig-lee-base}
#| fig-cap: "**Simulated data.** Option C: Lee's L between 1995 and each later snapshot. Top: global L. Bottom: local L within 360 m."
#| fig-width: 7.5
#| fig-height: 5.6
lee_figure("base", "Comparison")
```

## Choosing the neighbourhood size {#sec-lee-scale}

Lee's L depends on the neighbourhood it averages over.
It is the correlation between the neighbourhood-averaged values, multiplied by a factor for each map that measures how spatially smooth it is at that neighbourhood size.
That factor shrinks as neighbourhoods widen, so values computed with different neighbourhoods cannot be compared with each other.

An obvious candidate is the Omniscape moving-window radius, but the larger of our two radii (42.9 km) is a poor choice:

- Each cell's current already sums the flow from every source within that radius.
  Averaging it again over the same area means each local L describes the whole region that produced the value, so it mostly reflects how much habitat there is regionally, and the corridor-scale pattern that makes local L worth mapping is lost.
- L shrinks towards zero as the neighbourhood widens, so values at that scale would be small and the local maps nearly uniform.
- At 90 m it is about 700,000 neighbours per cell, which cannot be computed without heavy aggregation.

The smaller radius, 2.57 km, is easier to defend.
It is the largest nearest-neighbour gap between old-forest patches, so it ties the neighbourhood to the scale at which patches link up, and it makes a reasonable upper bound.

Rather than fix one value in advance, we can compute L across a range of neighbourhood sizes and look at how it changes (@fig-lee-scale).
A size where the curve levels off, or one with an ecological meaning, can then be chosen, and the figure itself shows how much the conclusions depend on that choice.

```{r lee-scale}
## Global L only (no permutation test), so wide neighbourhoods stay cheap
radii <- c(1, 2, 4, 6, 8, 12, 16)
lee_scale <- dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(radii, function(k) {
  lw_k <- spdep::nb2listw(spdep::dnearneigh(xy, 0, k * RES * 1.001), style = "W")
  L <- function(x, y) spdep::lee(x, y, lw_k, n = length(x))$L
  data.frame(
    radius = k * RES,
    `B: consecutive (mean of six)` = mean(vapply(
      comparisons$consec, function(p) L(p$x, p$y), numeric(1)
    )),
    `C: 1995 against 2025` = L(lcum[[1]], lcum[[length(lcum)]]),
    check.names = FALSE
  )
})) |>
  tidyr::pivot_longer(-radius, names_to = "comparison", values_to = "L")
L_at <- function(cmp, r) sprintf("%.2f", lee_scale$L[lee_scale$comparison == cmp & lee_scale$radius == r])
```

```{r fig-lee-scale}
#| fig-cap: "**Simulated data.** Global Lee's L against neighbourhood radius, for two of the comparisons above. The dashed line marks the scale (one standard deviation of the Gaussian window) at which the simulation builds flow potential, the stand-in for Omniscape's moving window."
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-height: 3.6
ggplot(lee_scale, aes(radius, L, colour = comparison, shape = comparison)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 8 * RES, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey50") +
  annotate("text", x = 8 * RES, y = Inf, label = "simulated window", vjust = 1.5, hjust = -0.05, size = 3, colour = "grey35") +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.7) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("#D55E00", "#009E73"), name = NULL) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c(16, 17), name = NULL) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = radii * RES) +
  labs(x = "Neighbourhood radius (m)", y = "Lee's L (global)") +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom", axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1)) +
  sim_caption()
```

In the simulation, the mean consecutive L falls from `r L_at("B: consecutive (mean of six)", 90)` at 90 m to `r L_at("B: consecutive (mean of six)", 1440)` at 1.44 km, and L between 1995 and 2025 from `r L_at("C: 1995 against 2025", 90)` to `r L_at("C: 1995 against 2025", 1440)`.

## Choices for the team

- **Which of options A to C.**
  They are not alternatives so much as answers to different questions: which years were unusual (A), when the pattern changed (B), and how far it has moved (C).
- **Neighbourhood size** (@sec-lee-scale).
  Not the 42.9 km Omniscape radius; the 2.57 km nearest-neighbour radius as an upper bound, with the final choice informed by a scale-sensitivity curve on the real surfaces.
- **Resolution.**
  A district raster has many more cells than this example.
  Aggregating to a coarser grid first, or using a regular sample of cells, keeps the computation manageable; the permutation test scales well, but see @sec-appendix on the analytical test.

# Change in connectivity by disturbance agent {#sec-agents}

## What it measures

For each interval, the change in cumulative current at each cell, grouped by the stand-replacing agent that disturbed it during that interval: harvest, fire, beetle, or none.
This links connectivity change to its causes.

```{r agent-change}
change <- dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(seq_along(agents), function(k) {
  data.frame(
    cell = seq_along(agents[[k]]),
    interval = names(agents)[k],
    agent = factor(agents[[k]], levels = AGENTS),
    dcum = lcum[[k + 1]] - lcum[[k]],
    dflow = flow[[k + 1]] - flow[[k]]
  )
}))
med_pct <- function(ag) {
  sprintf(
    "%+.0f%%",
    100 * (2^stats::median(change$dcum[change$agent == ag]) - 1)
  )
}
med_norm <- function(ag) {
  sprintf("%.2f", stats::median(change$dflow[change$agent == ag]))
}

## distance from each cell to the nearest cell disturbed in the same interval, and by which agent
nearest <- dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(seq_along(agents), function(k) {
  present <- setdiff(unique(agents[[k]]), "None")
  d <- sapply(present, function(ag) {
    r <- template
    terra::values(r) <- ifelse(agents[[k]] == ag, 1, NA)
    terra::values(terra::distance(r), mat = FALSE)
  })
  d <- matrix(d, ncol = length(present), dimnames = list(NULL, present))
  data.frame(
    interval = names(agents)[k],
    cell = seq_len(nrow(d)),
    disturbed = agents[[k]] != "None",
    nearest_agent = factor(
      present[max.col(-d, ties.method = "first")],
      levels = AGENTS
    ),
    dist = apply(d, 1, min),
    dcum = lcum[[k + 1]] - lcum[[k]]
  )
}))
```

```{r agent-model}
## Replicates are landscape-unit means, not pixels: cells are spatially autocorrelated and each
## appears in every interval. Units with fewer than 10 cells of an agent in an interval are dropped.
lu_means <- change |>
  dplyr::mutate(lu = lu[cell]) |>
  dplyr::group_by(lu, interval, agent) |>
  dplyr::summarise(dcum = mean(dcum), ncell = dplyr::n(), .groups = "drop") |>
  dplyr::filter(ncell >= 10) |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    interval = factor(interval),
    group = interaction(agent, interval, drop = TRUE, sep = ":")
  )

## Main effects: additive model
m_add <- lmerTest::lmer(dcum ~ agent + interval + (1 | lu), data = lu_means)
a_add <- stats::anova(m_add)

## One mean per observed agent x interval combination, so the comparisons below use only the
## combinations that occur (fire, for one, is missing from four intervals)
m_cell <- lmerTest::lmer(dcum ~ 0 + group + (1 | lu), data = lu_means)
grp <- levels(lu_means$group)
stopifnot(identical(names(lme4::fixef(m_cell)), paste0("group", grp)))

## contrast weights over the group means
cvec <- function(w) {
  v <- stats::setNames(numeric(length(grp)), grp)
  for (k in names(w)) v[k] <- v[k] + w[[k]]
  v
}
## agent minus undisturbed, within one interval
effect_w <- function(ag, iv) stats::setNames(c(1, -1), paste(c(ag, "None"), iv, sep = ":"))

DISTURBED <- setdiff(AGENTS, "None")
intervals_with <- function(ag) {
  Filter(function(iv) all(paste(c(ag, "None"), iv, sep = ":") %in% grp), levels(lu_means$interval))
}

## Each agent against undisturbed cells in the same interval, Holm-adjusted across all of them
contrasts <- dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(DISTURBED, function(ag) {
  dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(intervals_with(ag), function(iv) {
    t <- lmerTest::contest(m_cell, cvec(effect_w(ag, iv)), joint = FALSE)
    data.frame(
      interval = iv, agent = ag, est = t$Estimate, t = t$`t value`, df = t$df, p = t$`Pr(>|t|)`,
      units = sum(lu_means$group == paste(ag, iv, sep = ":"))
    )
  }))
})) |>
  dplyr::mutate(p_adj = stats::p.adjust(p, method = "holm"))

## Does each agent's effect differ among intervals? Joint test that every interval's effect equals
## the first interval's.
between <- dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(DISTURBED, function(ag) {
  ivs <- intervals_with(ag)
  if (length(ivs) < 2) {
    return(NULL)
  }
  L <- do.call(rbind, lapply(ivs[-1], function(iv) {
    cvec(c(effect_w(ag, iv), -effect_w(ag, ivs[1])))
  }))
  t <- lmerTest::contest(m_cell, L, joint = TRUE)
  data.frame(
    term = paste(ag, "effect differs among intervals"),
    F = t$`F value`, df1 = t$NumDF, df2 = t$DenDF, p = t$`Pr(>F)`
  )
}))

anova_tbl <- dplyr::bind_rows(
  data.frame(
    term = c("Agent", "Interval"),
    F = a_add$`F value`, df1 = a_add$NumDF, df2 = a_add$DenDF, p = a_add$`Pr(>F)`
  ),
  between
)

stars <- function(p) {
  as.character(cut(p, c(-Inf, 0.001, 0.01, 0.05, Inf), labels = c("***", "**", "*", "ns")))
}
fmt_p <- function(p) format.pval(p, digits = 2, eps = 0.001)
```

```{r fig-agent-box}
#| fig-cap: "**Simulated data.** Change in cumulative current over each five-year interval, for cells disturbed during that interval by each agent, and for undisturbed cells. Boxes show the cells (interquartile range; whiskers to 1.5 times it); black dots are landscape-unit means, the replicates the statistical model uses. Stars give the difference from undisturbed cells in the same interval (@tbl-agent-contrasts), Holm-adjusted: * p < 0.05, ** p < 0.01, *** p < 0.001, ns not significant. Intervals with no disturbance by an agent have no box for it; a box with no dots or stars had too few cells in any landscape unit to form a replicate."
#| fig-width: 7.5
#| fig-height: 4.6
ylim_box <- stats::quantile(change$dcum, c(0.005, 0.995))
star_df <- contrasts |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    agent = factor(agent, levels = AGENTS),
    label = stars(p_adj),
    ## above the bulk of the data, in headroom added to the panel below
    y = ylim_box[2] + 0.06 * diff(ylim_box)
  )

ggplot(change, aes(agent, dcum, fill = agent)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey50") +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.shape = NA, width = 0.6, linewidth = 0.3) +
  geom_point(
    data = lu_means, aes(agent, dcum), inherit.aes = FALSE,
    position = position_jitter(width = 0.15, height = 0, seed = 1), size = 0.7, colour = "grey10"
  ) +
  geom_text(data = star_df, aes(agent, y, label = label), inherit.aes = FALSE, size = 3.2, vjust = 0.5) +
  facet_wrap(~interval, nrow = 2) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = AGENT_COLOURS, guide = "none") +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = log2(c(0.125, 0.25, 0.5, 1, 2)), labels = pct_lab) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(ylim_box[1], ylim_box[2] + 0.1 * diff(ylim_box))) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Change in cumulative current") +
  sim_caption()
```

@fig-agent-box is the direct version: disturbed cells lose flow, and the useful comparison is between agents, and between intervals for the same agent.
The median change in the simulation is `r med_pct("Harvest")` for harvest, `r med_pct("Beetle")` for beetle and `r med_pct("Fire")` for fire.

The choice of layer matters here.
Measured in normalized current, the same fire cells change by a median of only `r med_norm("Fire")`, against `r med_norm("Harvest")` for harvest, which would make fire look the least damaging agent.
That is an artefact of the ratio: a large burn removes the sources over the whole neighbourhood, so flow and flow potential fall together, while a cutblock is a young cell in a neighbourhood whose potential is largely intact.

## Testing differences among agents and intervals {#sec-agent-model}

The comparison in @fig-agent-box can be tested formally, but not with the cells as replicates.
Neighbouring cells are strongly autocorrelated and each cell appears in every interval, so an ANOVA on cells would treat tens of thousands of dependent values as independent and find almost any difference significant.

The structure proposed here:

- **Replicate:** the mean change over the cells of one agent, in one reporting area, in one interval.
  Here the reporting areas are landscape units, and an area needs at least 10 cells of an agent in an interval to count.
- **Response:** change in log cumulative current over the interval.
- **Fixed effects:** disturbance agent (none, harvest, fire, beetle) and interval.
- **Random effect:** an intercept for each landscape unit, because the same unit contributes to every interval and agent.
- **Comparisons:** each agent against *undisturbed* cells in the same interval.
  Comparing within the interval removes change that happens everywhere, such as stands ageing into higher source weight.
  These comparisons give the stars in @fig-agent-box, adjusted for multiple comparisons by Holm's method.

The design is unbalanced and incomplete: harvest occurs in every interval, beetle in four, and fire in two.
A single agent-by-interval interaction term cannot be estimated where combinations are missing, so whether each agent's effect changes over time is tested agent by agent, using only the intervals where it occurs.
@tbl-agent-anova gives the F tests and @tbl-agent-contrasts the individual comparisons.

```{r tbl-agent-anova}
#| tbl-cap: "**Simulated data.** F tests from the mixed model. Degrees of freedom by Satterthwaite's method."
anova_tbl |>
  dplyr::transmute(
    Term = term,
    F = sprintf("%.1f", F),
    df = sprintf("%d, %.0f", as.integer(df1), df2),
    p = fmt_p(p)
  ) |>
  knitr::kable(format = "pipe", align = "lrrr")
```

```{r tbl-agent-contrasts}
#| tbl-cap: "**Simulated data.** Change in cumulative current for each agent relative to undisturbed cells in the same interval (ratio of geometric means), with Holm-adjusted p-values. Units: landscape units contributing a mean."
contrasts |>
  dplyr::transmute(
    Interval = interval,
    Agent = agent,
    `Relative change` = sprintf("%+.0f%%", 100 * (2^est - 1)),
    t = sprintf("%.1f", t),
    df = sprintf("%.0f", df),
    `p (Holm)` = fmt_p(p_adj),
    Units = units
  ) |>
  knitr::kable(format = "pipe", align = "llrrrrr")
```

Every comparison is highly significant in the simulation, because the simulated effects are large and uniform.
On real data, the number of reporting areas and the variation between them will decide that.

Points to settle before applying this:

- **Fire is a handful of events.**
  Each interval's fire is one fire, so "fire in 2015--2020" cannot be separated from that particular fire, and its landscape units are not independent of one another.
  The same applies, less severely, to a beetle outbreak.
  If the disturbance record identifies individual events (each cutblock or fire), events could be the replicate instead, with landscape unit as a grouping above them.
- **Spatial dependence between units.**
  Neighbouring landscape units are themselves correlated.
  A spatially structured random effect would address this; with a few dozen units it may not be estimable, and the p-values should be read as approximate.
- **Pixel-level alternative.**
  A regular sample of cells spaced farther apart than the autocorrelation range of the current surface, with cell as a random effect across intervals, uses the cells directly while keeping them close to independent.
- **Checks.** Residuals should be inspected for skew and unequal variance between agents; the log ratio helps, but unequal variances may need modelling.

The less obvious effect is on the cells **around** a disturbance.
Omniscape is not a cell-by-cell model: a disturbance removes sources and raises resistance, which changes the flow through the forest around it as well.
A cell-only summary credits that change to "no disturbance".
@fig-agent-distance shows it by distance from the nearest disturbance in the same interval.

```{r fig-agent-distance}
#| fig-cap: "**Simulated data.** Mean change in cumulative current against distance from the nearest cell disturbed in the same interval, by the agent of that disturbance, pooled over intervals. Distance 0 is the disturbed cells themselves."
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-height: 3.6
bins <- c(-1, 0, 90, 180, 360, 540, 720, 1080, 1440, Inf)
dd <- nearest |>
  dplyr::filter(!is.na(nearest_agent)) |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    band = cut(
      dist,
      bins,
      labels = c(0, 90, 180, 360, 540, 720, 1080, 1440, 2000)
    ),
    band = as.numeric(as.character(band))
  ) |>
  dplyr::group_by(nearest_agent, band) |>
  dplyr::summarise(dcum = mean(dcum), n = dplyr::n(), .groups = "drop") |>
  dplyr::filter(n >= 30)
## for the text: harvest, 180-360 m from the edge
dd_reach_pct <- pct_lab(dd$dcum[dd$nearest_agent == "Harvest" & dd$band == 360])
dd_far_pct <- pct_lab(dd$dcum[dd$nearest_agent == "Harvest" & dd$band == 2000])

ggplot(dd, aes(band, dcum, colour = nearest_agent)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey50") +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.7) +
  geom_point(size = 1.8) +
  scale_colour_manual(
    values = AGENT_COLOURS[-1],
    name = "Nearest disturbance"
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = PCT_BREAKS, labels = pct_lab) +
  labs(
    x = "Distance to nearest disturbance (m, upper edge of band)",
    y = "Mean change in cumulative current"
  ) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom") +
  sim_caption()
```

In the simulation, cells 180--360 m from a harvest edge change by `r dd_reach_pct` on average, against `r dd_far_pct` beyond 1.4 km, where the stands are simply ageing.

## Dominant agent by reporting area

At the cell level each cell has at most one stand-replacing agent per interval, so "dominant" only means something once cells are grouped into reporting areas.
@fig-agent-lu does this for landscape units: each point is a unit, placed by how much of it was disturbed over the series and how much its cumulative current changed, and coloured by the agent that disturbed the most area.

```{r fig-agent-lu}
#| fig-cap: "**Simulated data.** Landscape units: share of area disturbed 1995-2025 (cells disturbed twice count twice) against mean change in cumulative current, coloured by the agent that disturbed the most area. Mean change is the geometric mean of the per-cell ratios."
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-height: 4.2
lu_agent <- dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(agents, function(a) {
  data.frame(lu = lu, agent = a)
})) |>
  dplyr::filter(agent != "None") |>
  dplyr::count(lu, agent) |>
  dplyr::left_join(
    as.data.frame(table(lu = lu), responseName = "ncell"),
    by = "lu"
  ) |>
  dplyr::group_by(lu) |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    disturbed = sum(n) / ncell[1],
    dominant = agent[which.max(n)],
    .groups = "drop"
  )
lu_change <- data.frame(lu = lu, dcum = lcum[[7]] - lcum[[1]]) |>
  dplyr::group_by(lu) |>
  dplyr::summarise(dcum = mean(dcum))
lu_df <- dplyr::left_join(lu_change, lu_agent, by = "lu") |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    disturbed = dplyr::coalesce(disturbed, 0),
    dominant = factor(dplyr::coalesce(dominant, "None"), levels = AGENTS)
  )

ggplot(lu_df, aes(disturbed, dcum, colour = dominant)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey60") +
  geom_point(size = 2.6) +
  ggrepel::geom_text_repel(
    aes(label = lu),
    size = 2.6,
    colour = "grey25",
    seed = 1
  ) +
  scale_colour_manual(
    values = AGENT_COLOURS,
    name = "Dominant agent",
    drop = TRUE
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::label_percent()) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = PCT_BREAKS, labels = pct_lab) +
  labs(
    x = "Area disturbed, 1995-2025",
    y = "Mean change in cumulative current"
  ) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom") +
  sim_caption()
```

## Choices for the team

- **What "dominant" means.**
  The agent covering the most area (as in @fig-agent-lu), or the agent with the largest summed effect on current; and over the whole series or per interval.
  The reporting areas are a separate choice (@sec-areas).
- **Disturbances below the stand-replacing threshold.**
  Partial beetle mortality and low-severity fire change resistance without resetting age.
  As set up in the series they are not distinguished, and they would fall into "None" here.
- **Attribution in the 2000 snapshot is weak.**
  The disturbance record only partly covers the start of the beetle outbreak, so 1995--2000 and 2000--2005 under-assign beetle until national disturbance data are added.
- **Including the neighbourhood effect.**
  We should decide whether to report a single "effect of harvest" that includes the surrounding change (e.g. all cells within a set distance), or the two components separately.

# Transitions between connectivity classes {#sec-transitions}

## What it measures

The connectivity class of each cell, followed through the series.
LandR's vegetation-transition plots [using the alluvial plots of @Brunson:2020] do this for leading vegetation type; the same plot works for any categorical map, including the four connectivity classes.

The classes are defined on normalized current, so this section uses it.
As @sec-layer explains, a cell moving from Diffuse to Channelized means its share of the local flow rose, not necessarily that more movement passes through it.

@fig-class-area is the simplest summary: the share of the landscape in each class at each snapshot.
It shows the net change but hides the exchanges -- a class can hold its area while the cells in it turn over completely.

```{r fig-class-area}
#| fig-cap: "**Simulated data.** Share of the landscape in each connectivity class at each snapshot."
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-height: 3.4
ca <- cells |>
  dplyr::count(epoch, class) |>
  dplyr::group_by(epoch) |>
  dplyr::mutate(share = n / sum(n))
ggplot(ca, aes(factor(epoch), share, fill = class)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.75, colour = "grey40", linewidth = 0.2) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = CONN_COLOURS, name = NULL) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_percent(), expand = c(0, 0)) +
  labs(x = "Snapshot", y = "Share of landscape") +
  sim_caption()
```

## Transition plots

@fig-alluvial follows cells through all seven snapshots, split by BEC zone as LandR does by reporting zone.
Each band is a set of cells that took the same path through the classes; its width is their area.

```{r fig-alluvial}
#| fig-cap: "**Simulated data.** Transitions between connectivity classes across the series, for two simulated BEC zones. Band width is area. Bands are grouped by the path cells took through all seven snapshots."
#| fig-width: 7.5
#| fig-height: 5.6
paths <- cells |>
  dplyr::select(cell, zone, epoch, class) |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(
    names_from = epoch,
    values_from = class,
    names_prefix = "y"
  ) |>
  dplyr::count(zone, dplyr::across(dplyr::starts_with("y")), name = "n") |>
  dplyr::mutate(path = dplyr::row_number(), area_km2 = n * RES^2 / 1e6)

lodes <- paths |>
  tidyr::pivot_longer(
    dplyr::starts_with("y"),
    names_to = "epoch",
    values_to = "class"
  ) |>
  dplyr::mutate(epoch = factor(sub("^y", "", epoch), levels = EPOCHS))

ggplot(
  lodes,
  aes(x = epoch, stratum = class, alluvium = path, y = area_km2, fill = class)
) +
  ## no `colour = NA` here: with ggplot2 4 it stops the flows drawing at all
  ggalluvial::geom_flow(alpha = 0.6) +
  ggalluvial::geom_stratum(width = 1 / 5, colour = "grey30", linewidth = 0.2) +
  facet_wrap(~zone, ncol = 1, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = CONN_COLOURS, name = NULL) +
  labs(x = "Snapshot", y = expression("Area (km"^2 * ")")) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom", panel.grid = element_blank()) +
  sim_caption()
```

With seven snapshots and four classes the diagram gets busy, and on real data most of the width is cells that stay Diffuse throughout.
Two complementary views of the same information are easier to read for a single pair of years, or for persistence.

```{r fig-transition-matrix}
#| fig-cap: "**Simulated data.** Left: where the area in each 1995 class ended up in 2025, as a share of the 1995 class. Right: number of snapshots, of seven, in which each cell was Intensified or Channelized."
#| fig-width: 7.5
#| fig-height: 3.6
tm <- data.frame(from = conn[[1]], to = conn[[7]]) |>
  dplyr::count(from, to, .drop = FALSE) |>
  dplyr::group_by(from) |>
  dplyr::mutate(share = n / sum(n))

p_tm <- ggplot(
  tm,
  aes(to, factor(from, levels = rev(CONN_CLASSES)), fill = share)
) +
  geom_tile(colour = "white", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_text(
    aes(
      label = scales::label_percent(accuracy = 1)(share),
      colour = share > 0.5
    ),
    size = 3
  ) +
  scale_fill_gradient(
    low = "#F7F7F7",
    high = "#2166AC",
    labels = scales::label_percent(),
    guide = "none"
  ) +
  scale_colour_manual(
    values = c(`TRUE` = "white", `FALSE` = "grey15"),
    guide = "none"
  ) +
  labs(x = "Class in 2025", y = "Class in 1995", title = "1995 to 2025") +
  theme(
    panel.grid = element_blank(),
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 30, hjust = 1)
  )

persist_n <- Reduce(
  `+`,
  lapply(conn, function(k) k %in% c("Intensified", "Channelized"))
)
persist <- data.frame(
  x = xy[, 1],
  y = xy[, 2],
  n = factor(persist_n, levels = 0:7)
)
p_pe <- map_layer(persist, "n", "Corridor persistence") +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c(
      "#F7F7F7",
      grDevices::colorRampPalette(c("#D1E5F0", "#053061"))(7)
    ),
    name = "Snapshots",
    drop = FALSE
  )

p_tm + p_pe + patchwork::plot_layout(widths = c(1, 1)) + sim_annotation()
```

The transition matrix in @fig-transition-matrix gives the 1995-to-2025 exchange as numbers that can go in a table.
The persistence map picks out corridors that held through the whole series against those that appeared or vanished, which is probably the most direct product for planning.

## Choices for the team

- **All seven snapshots or a subset.** The alluvial plot is clearer with three or four (e.g. 1995, 2010, 2025).
- **Agreement statistics.** Cohen's kappa [@Cohen:1960] between pairs of class maps is a one-number summary of class stability, and we already use it for the resolution comparison.
- **Class edges.** Cells near a threshold flip class with small changes in flow; the persistence map and the transition counts both inherit this.
  A minimum change, or a buffer around the cut-offs, would separate real transitions from noise.

# Patch metrics {#sec-fragstats}

## What it measures

Patch layers can be summarized directly with landscape pattern metrics, the set popularized by FRAGSTATS [@McGarigal:1995] and available in R through landscapemetrics [@Hesselbarth:2019].
These describe the amount and arrangement of patches at each snapshot, without any model of movement.
They are cheap to compute, familiar to reviewers, and comparable to other studies.

@tbl-metrics lists a candidate set that bears on connectivity.
FRAGSTATS also has a "connectance" index, defined by a threshold distance between patches; landscapemetrics does not implement it, but the pipeline's interpatch-distance chain measures much the same thing on the actual polygons.

```{r tbl-metrics}
#| tbl-cap: "Candidate class-level metrics."
metric_tbl <- data.frame(
  Metric = c(
    "Percentage of landscape (PLAND)",
    "Number of patches (NP)",
    "Largest patch index (LPI)",
    "Core area percentage (CPLAND)",
    "Mean nearest-neighbour distance (ENN)",
    "Patch cohesion (COHESION)",
    "Effective mesh size (MESH)",
    "Aggregation index (AI)"
  ),
  Meaning = c(
    "Amount of the class",
    "Count of separate patches; rises with fragmentation, falls with outright loss",
    "Share of the landscape in the single largest patch",
    "Interior area beyond an edge depth, as a share of the landscape",
    "Mean edge-to-edge distance from each patch to the nearest of the same class",
    "Physical connectedness of the class; near 100 when patches are large and compact",
    "Expected size of the patch a randomly placed point falls in; drops sharply as large patches split",
    "How clumped the class's cells are, relative to the most clumped arrangement possible"
  )
)
knitr::kable(metric_tbl, format = "pipe")
```

## Which pixels make a patch?

The metrics are only as meaningful as the patch definition, and there is more than one reasonable choice.
Each answers a slightly different question:

1. **Old and mature forest patches**, as the pipeline already defines them (by BEC variant and natural disturbance type, with minimum sizes).
   This is the habitat the analysis is about, and it is what most readers will expect.
2. **Interior old forest**: the same patches less an edge buffer.
   Interior area is often what drops first, and the pipeline already computes it.
3. **High source weight**: cells above a source-weight threshold.
   These are the cells Omniscape starts movement from, so the patches match the model exactly, including non-forest habitat that carries source weight.
4. **Low resistance**: cells below a resistance threshold, from the resistance map that went into Omniscape.
   This is the landscape that is easy to move *through*, which includes matrix that is not habitat (e.g. mid-seral forest); it describes permeability rather than habitat.
5. **Corridor patches from Omniscape**: cells classed Intensified or Channelized.
   Patch metrics on these describe the corridor network itself -- how much there is, and whether it is breaking up -- and pair naturally with the persistence map in @fig-transition-matrix.

For any of the threshold-based definitions (3--5), the threshold has to stay fixed across snapshots, or a change in the threshold is read as a change in the landscape.
@fig-patchdefs shows four metrics under each definition on the simulated landscape.

```{r patch-metrics}
## Patch metrics on a two-class raster (1 = patch, 0 = not), class 1 only
lsm_patch <- function(is_patch, what, mask = NULL) {
  r <- template
  v <- as.integer(is_patch)
  if (!is.null(mask)) {
    v[!mask] <- NA
  }
  terra::values(r) <- v
  landscapemetrics::calculate_lsm(
    r,
    what = what,
    edge_depth = 1,
    directions = 8
  ) |>
    dplyr::filter(class == 1)
}

seral_rasters <- lapply(ages, function(a) {
  r <- template
  terra::values(r) <- as.integer(seral_of(a))
  r
})

METRICS <- c(
  "lsm_c_pland",
  "lsm_c_np",
  "lsm_c_lpi",
  "lsm_c_cpland",
  "lsm_c_enn_mn",
  "lsm_c_cohesion",
  "lsm_c_mesh",
  "lsm_c_ai"
)
pm <- dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(seq_along(EPOCHS), function(i) {
  landscapemetrics::calculate_lsm(
    seral_rasters[[i]],
    what = METRICS,
    edge_depth = 1,
    directions = 8
  ) |>
    dplyr::mutate(epoch = EPOCHS[i])
})) |>
  dplyr::mutate(seral = SERAL_CLASSES[class]) |>
  dplyr::filter(seral %in% c("Mature", "Old"))

## an old-forest metric value for inline text, rounded for reading
om <- function(m, yr) {
  v <- pm$value[pm$seral == "Old" & pm$metric == m & pm$epoch == yr]
  format(signif(v, 3), big.mark = ",")
}

## Thresholds fixed across snapshots. In the simulation resistance is 1 / conductance.
SRC_MIN <- 0.3
RES_MAX <- 2
patch_defs <- list(
  "Old forest" = function(i) ages[[i]] >= 140,
  "High source weight" = function(i) source_wt(ages[[i]]) >= SRC_MIN,
  "Low resistance" = function(i) 1 / conductance(ages[[i]]) <= RES_MAX,
  "Corridors (Omniscape)" = function(i) {
    conn[[i]] %in% c("Intensified", "Channelized")
  }
)
pdefs <- dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(names(patch_defs), function(def) {
  dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(seq_along(EPOCHS), function(i) {
    lsm_patch(
      patch_defs[[def]](i),
      c("lsm_c_pland", "lsm_c_np", "lsm_c_mesh", "lsm_c_enn_mn")
    ) |>
      dplyr::mutate(definition = def, epoch = EPOCHS[i])
  }))
}))
```

```{r fig-patchdefs}
#| fig-cap: "**Simulated data.** Four patch metrics under four patch definitions, with thresholds held fixed across snapshots: old forest (140 years and older), source weight of at least 0.3, resistance of at most 2 (simulation units), and cells classed Intensified or Channelized."
#| fig-width: 7.5
#| fig-height: 4.6
def_labels <- c(
  pland = "Percentage of landscape (%)",
  np = "Number of patches",
  mesh = "Effective mesh size (ha)",
  enn_mn = "Mean nearest-neighbour dist. (m)"
)
pdefs$metric <- factor(def_labels[pdefs$metric], levels = def_labels)
pdefs$definition <- factor(pdefs$definition, levels = names(patch_defs))

ggplot(pdefs, aes(epoch, value, colour = definition, shape = definition)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.7) +
  geom_point(size = 1.8) +
  facet_wrap(~metric, scales = "free_y", ncol = 2) +
  scale_colour_manual(
    values = stats::setNames(
      c("#009E73", "#CC79A7", "#D55E00", "#0072B2"),
      names(patch_defs)
    ),
    name = NULL
  ) +
  scale_shape_manual(
    values = stats::setNames(c(16, 17, 15, 18), names(patch_defs)),
    name = NULL
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(1995, 2010, 2025)) +
  labs(x = "Snapshot", y = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom") +
  guides(colour = guide_legend(nrow = 2), shape = guide_legend(nrow = 2)) +
  sim_caption()
```

```{r patchdef-text}
pd <- function(def, m, yr) {
  v <- pdefs$value[
    pdefs$definition == def &
      pdefs$metric == def_labels[[m]] &
      pdefs$epoch == yr
  ]
  format(signif(v, 3), big.mark = ",")
}
```

The definitions disagree in ways that matter.
In the simulation, old forest falls from `r pd("Old forest", "pland", 1995)`% to `r pd("Old forest", "pland", 2025)`% of the landscape, low-resistance land from `r pd("Low resistance", "pland", 1995)`% to `r pd("Low resistance", "pland", 2025)`%, and corridor cells go from `r pd("Corridors (Omniscape)", "pland", 1995)`% to `r pd("Corridors (Omniscape)", "pland", 2025)`%.
High source weight is close to old forest here only because the simulation derives source weight from stand age alone; in the real data the two differ wherever non-forest habitat carries source weight.
Corridor area can *grow* while habitat shrinks, because as forest is lost the flow concentrates into what remains; the corridor metrics describe the network the model routes movement through, not the habitat behind it.

## Old and mature forest in more detail

@fig-metrics shows all eight metrics for old and mature forest (definition 1).

```{r fig-metrics}
#| fig-cap: "**Simulated data.** Class-level landscape metrics for old and mature forest at each snapshot, with cells joined to all eight neighbours and a one-cell (90 m) edge depth for core area."
#| fig-width: 7.5
#| fig-height: 5
metric_labels <- c(
  pland = "Percentage of landscape (%)",
  np = "Number of patches",
  lpi = "Largest patch index (%)",
  cpland = "Core area percentage (%)",
  enn_mn = "Mean nearest-neighbour dist. (m)",
  cohesion = "Patch cohesion",
  mesh = "Effective mesh size (ha)",
  ai = "Aggregation index (%)"
)
pm_plot <- dplyr::mutate(
  pm,
  metric = factor(metric_labels[metric], levels = metric_labels)
)

ggplot(pm_plot, aes(epoch, value, colour = seral)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.7) +
  geom_point(size = 1.6) +
  facet_wrap(~metric, scales = "free_y", ncol = 4) +
  scale_colour_manual(
    values = c(Mature = "#31A354", Old = "#00441B"),
    name = NULL
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(1995, 2010, 2025)) +
  labs(x = "Snapshot", y = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom") +
  sim_caption()
```

In the simulation, old forest falls from `r om("pland", 1995)`% to `r om("pland", 2025)`% of the landscape, and its number of patches rises from `r om("np", 1995)` to `r om("np", 2025)` as large patches break up.
Effective mesh size shows the break-up most strongly, falling from `r om("mesh", 1995)` ha to `r om("mesh", 2025)` ha, while cohesion barely moves (`r om("cohesion", 1995)` to `r om("cohesion", 2025)`).
Mean nearest-neighbour distance *falls*, from `r om("enn_mn", 1995)` m to `r om("enn_mn", 2025)` m, because the fragments of a broken patch sit close to one another.
A shorter distance here is a sign of break-up, not of better connectivity, so distance metrics need reading alongside patch number and mesh size.
Patch number has the opposite ambiguity: it rises when patches split and falls when small ones are lost outright.

## Choices for the team

- **Which pixels make a patch** (definitions 1--5 above), and, for the threshold-based ones, which threshold.
  More than one can be reported; old forest and corridor patches together would show habitat and the network routed through it.
- **Rasterizing the patches.**
  The pipeline builds patches as polygons; these metrics work on rasters, so the pixel size and the eight- versus four-neighbour rule change patch counts and distances.
  Rasterizing at the same 30 m or 90 m as the Omniscape inputs would keep the two families consistent.
- **Edge depth for core area.**
  The pipeline already defines interior forest; the core-area metrics should use the same edge depth.
- **Landscape boundary.**
  Patches cut by the district boundary look smaller and more isolated than they are.
  A buffered landscape, or excluding boundary patches from distance metrics, avoids this.
- **How many metrics.**
  Many of these are strongly correlated.
  Three or four -- amount, patch number, mesh size, and a distance measure -- probably cover what the others say.
  Cohesion barely moved in the simulation while the old forest lost most of its mesh size, which suggests it is the least informative here.

# Summaries by reporting area {#sec-areas}

Almost every summary above can be broken down by reporting area, and for planning that is usually the form that gets used.
We assume BEC zone and landscape unit will be among them.
The current-condition outputs already summarize normalized current per landscape unit x BEC zone combination, and inside versus outside moose wetlands, mule deer winter ranges, old growth management areas, parks, wetlands and wildlife habitat areas; any of these could be carried through the series too.

@tbl-areas lists, for each method, what a per-area summary would be and what to watch for.

```{r tbl-areas}
#| tbl-cap: "Summaries by reporting area, by method."
areas_tbl <- data.frame(
  Method = c(
    "Change in cumulative current",
    "Lee's L",
    "Change by disturbance agent",
    "Class shares and transitions",
    "Corridor persistence",
    "Patch metrics",
    "Per-cell trends"
  ),
  `Per-area summary` = c(
    "Mean percentage change; share of area losing more than a set amount",
    "Global L within each area, or mean local L",
    "Dominant agent; change against area disturbed",
    "Class shares per snapshot; transition matrix or alluvial plot per area",
    "Share of area that was a corridor in all (or most) snapshots",
    "Class metrics on the patches within each area",
    "Share of area with a significant decline or increase"
  ),
  Caveat = c(
    "Small areas are dominated by edge effects of the moving window",
    "Needs enough cells per area; neighbours across the boundary are cut",
    "Dominance needs a rule (area or effect)",
    "Alluvial plots get unreadable with many areas",
    "Inherits class-edge noise",
    "Patches cut at area boundaries look smaller and more isolated; mesh and distance most affected",
    "Multiple-testing correction across cells"
  ),
  check.names = FALSE
)
knitr::kable(areas_tbl, format = "pipe")
```

@fig-areas shows two of these on the simulated landscape units and zones.

```{r fig-areas}
#| fig-cap: "**Simulated data.** Left: mean change in cumulative current since 1995, by landscape unit and snapshot, grouped by the BEC zone each unit mostly falls in. Right: old-forest area and effective mesh size by BEC zone, with patches cut at the zone boundary."
#| fig-width: 7.5
#| fig-height: 4.6
lu_epoch <- cells |>
  dplyr::group_by(cell) |>
  dplyr::mutate(dcum = lcum - lcum[epoch == 1995]) |>
  dplyr::group_by(lu, epoch) |>
  dplyr::summarise(dcum = mean(dcum), .groups = "drop") |>
  dplyr::mutate(bec = lu_zone[lu])

p_heat <- ggplot(lu_epoch, aes(factor(epoch), lu, fill = dcum)) +
  geom_tile(colour = "white", linewidth = 0.4) +
  facet_grid(bec ~ ., scales = "free_y", space = "free_y") +
  diverging(
    1,
    "Change\nsince 1995",
    labels = pct_lab,
    breaks = log2(c(0.5, 0.8, 1, 1.25, 2))
  ) +
  labs(x = "Snapshot", y = NULL) +
  theme(
    panel.grid = element_blank(),
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1),
    legend.key.size = unit(0.35, "cm"),
    legend.text = element_text(size = 7)
  )

zone_pm <- dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(sort(unique(zone)), function(z) {
  dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(seq_along(EPOCHS), function(i) {
    lsm_patch(
      ages[[i]] >= 140,
      c("lsm_c_pland", "lsm_c_mesh"),
      mask = zone == z
    ) |>
      dplyr::mutate(zone = z, epoch = EPOCHS[i])
  }))
})) |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    metric = c(pland = "Old forest (%)", mesh = "Mesh size (ha)")[metric]
  )

p_zone <- ggplot(zone_pm, aes(epoch, value, colour = zone)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.7) +
  geom_point(size = 1.5) +
  facet_wrap(~metric, scales = "free_y", ncol = 1) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = ZONE_COLOURS, name = NULL) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(1995, 2010, 2025)) +

p_heat + p_zone + patchwork::plot_layout(widths = c(1.3, 1)) + sim_annotation()
```

# Other options worth considering {#sec-other}

## Per-cell trends

A rank-based trend at each cell across the seven snapshots gives a single map of the direction and rate of change: the Theil-Sen slope (the median of the slopes between every pair of snapshots), with a Mann-Kendall test for whether there is a monotonic trend at all.
With only seven points per cell the test has little power, and testing thousands of cells needs a correction for multiple testing; here the false discovery rate is controlled at 5%.

```{r trend}
lmat <- do.call(cbind, lcum)
pairs <- utils::combn(length(EPOCHS), 2)
slopes <- sapply(seq_len(ncol(pairs)), function(j) {
  (lmat[, pairs[2, j]] - lmat[, pairs[1, j]]) /
    (EPOCHS[pairs[2, j]] - EPOCHS[pairs[1, j]])
})
## per decade, as a log2 ratio
sen <- apply(slopes, 1, stats::median) * 10
mk_p <- apply(lmat, 1, function(v) {
  suppressWarnings(
    stats::cor.test(EPOCHS, v, method = "kendall", exact = TRUE)$p.value
  )
})
mk_q <- stats::p.adjust(mk_p, method = "BH")
trend <- data.frame(
  x = xy[, 1],
  y = xy[, 2],
  sen = sen,
  sig = ifelse(mk_q < 0.05, sen, NA)
)
share_sig_down <- mean(mk_q < 0.05 & sen < 0)
share_sig_up <- mean(mk_q < 0.05 & sen > 0)
```

```{r fig-trend}
#| fig-cap: "**Simulated data.** Left: Theil-Sen trend in cumulative current per decade, 1995-2025. Right: the same, showing only cells with a significant Mann-Kendall trend after false-discovery-rate correction (5%); grey cells have none."
#| fig-width: 7.5
#| fig-height: 3.6
lim_s <- stats::quantile(abs(trend$sen), 0.99)
sen_scale <- diverging(
   lim_s,
   "Change per\ndecade",
   labels = pct_lab,
   breaks = log2(c(0.5, 0.8, 1, 1.25, 2))
)
(map_layer(trend, "sen", "Theil-Sen trend") + sen_scale) +
   (map_layer(trend, "sig", "Significant trends only") +
      sen_scale +
      theme(panel.background = element_rect(fill = "grey85", colour = NA))) +
   patchwork::plot_layout(guides = "collect") +
   sim_annotation()
```

In the simulation `r scales::label_percent(accuracy = 1)(share_sig_down)` of cells have a significant decline and `r scales::label_percent(accuracy = 1)(share_sig_up)` a significant increase.
The trend map is the one-map summary of the whole series; it cannot show change that reverses partway (loss followed by recovery), which the snapshot comparisons in @sec-lee can.

## Linking the two families

The Omniscape surfaces and the patch metrics should tell a consistent story: where habitat was lost or broken up, modelled flow should fall.
Comparing the change in each over the same reporting areas tests that, and flags areas where the model responds differently from what the habitat change suggests.
@fig-link does this for the simulated landscape units.

```{r link}
lu_ids <- sort(unique(lu))
lu_pm <- dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(lu_ids, function(u) {
  dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(c(1, length(EPOCHS)), function(i) {
    lsm_patch(
      ages[[i]] >= 140,
      c("lsm_c_pland", "lsm_c_mesh"),
      mask = lu == u
    ) |>
      dplyr::mutate(lu = u, epoch = EPOCHS[i])
  }))
})) |>
  dplyr::select(lu, epoch, metric, value) |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = c(metric, epoch), values_from = value) |>
  ## a unit with no old forest left has no class-1 row, i.e. zero area and zero mesh
  dplyr::mutate(dplyr::across(
    dplyr::matches("^(pland|mesh)_"),
    ~ dplyr::coalesce(.x, 0)
  )) |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    d_pland = pland_2025 - pland_1995,
    ## mesh size can reach zero when the old forest in a unit is lost entirely
    d_mesh = log2((mesh_2025 + 1) / (mesh_1995 + 1))
  ) |>
  dplyr::left_join(lu_change, by = "lu") |>
  dplyr::mutate(bec = lu_zone[lu])

rho <- function(v) {
  sprintf("%.2f", stats::cor(lu_pm[[v]], lu_pm$dcum, method = "spearman"))
}
```

```{r fig-link}
#| fig-cap: "**Simulated data.** Landscape units: change in old-forest area (left) and in old-forest effective mesh size (right), 1995-2025, against mean change in cumulative current."
#| fig-width: 7.5
#| fig-height: 3.6
link_plot <- function(
  xvar,
  xlab,
  xlabels = ggplot2::waiver(),
  xbreaks = ggplot2::waiver()
) {
  ggplot(lu_pm, aes(.data[[xvar]], dcum, colour = bec)) +
    geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey60") +
    geom_point(size = 2.4) +
    scale_colour_manual(values = ZONE_COLOURS, name = "BEC zone") +
    scale_x_continuous(labels = xlabels, breaks = xbreaks) +
    scale_y_continuous(breaks = PCT_BREAKS, labels = pct_lab) +
    labs(x = xlab, y = "Mean change in cumulative current")
}
link_plot("d_pland", "Change in old forest (percentage points)") +
  link_plot(
    "d_mesh",
    "Change in old-forest mesh size",
    pct_lab,
    log2(c(0.125, 0.25, 0.5, 1, 2))
  ) +
  patchwork::plot_layout(guides = "collect") +
  sim_annotation() &
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

In the simulation the rank correlation between change in old-forest area and change in cumulative current across units is `r rho("d_pland")`, and `r rho("d_mesh")` for mesh size.
On real data, a unit well off the general relationship is worth a look: it may be where something other than old forest (resistance from roads, or non-forest sources) drives the change.
With a few dozen units, this is a descriptive check, not a test.

# Questions for the team

1. Do we agree to measure change in amount with cumulative current, and keep normalized current for the connectivity classes (@sec-layer)?
2. Which of the approaches are worth carrying to the real series?
3. For Lee's L: which of options A--C, and at what neighbourhood scale (up to the 2.57 km nearest-neighbour radius)?
4. For the disturbance analysis: how do we define the dominant agent, and do we report the change around disturbances separately? For the statistical test, what is the replicate -- reporting-area means, individual disturbance events, or a spaced sample of cells?
5. For transitions: all seven snapshots or a subset?
6. For patch metrics: which patch definition(s), and for threshold-based ones, which thresholds? Which three or four metrics, at what resolution and edge depth?
7. **What reporting areas do we care about?** We assume BEC zone and landscape unit will be included; which of the others (moose wetlands, mule deer winter ranges, OGMAs, parks, wetlands, WHAs, or others) should be carried through the series?

# Appendix: implementation notes {#sec-appendix}

```{r versions}
pkg_ver <- function(p) as.character(utils::packageVersion(p))
```

This appendix is for whoever implements the chosen methods.

- **Simulation.**
  All data are generated in the `simulate` chunk of this document from a fixed seed; nothing reads pipeline outputs.
  Normalized current is a cell's conductance divided by its Gaussian-weighted neighbourhood mean, raised to 0.75; flow potential is source weight summed over a Gaussian window; cumulative current is their product.
  Landscape units are the Voronoi cells of 16 random points.
- **Omniscape outputs.**
  The three surfaces are `cum_currmap.tif`, `flow_potential.tif` and `normalized_cum_currmap.tif` in each run directory.
  Each epoch's run takes its own `resistance_composite_<epoch>_*.tif` and `sourcewt_composite_<epoch>_*.tif`; the radius comes from the district's pinned interpatch-distance quantiles and does not vary by epoch.
  The existing zonal summaries (`zonal_summaries()`) read only `normalized_cum_currmap.tif`.
- **Lee's L** uses spdep (`r pkg_ver("spdep")`), on log2 cumulative current.
  `spdep::lee.mc()` runs the permutation test and `spdep::lee()` returns the local values.
  Avoid `spdep::lee.test()`, the analytical test, on raster data: it builds a dense cell-by-cell matrix.
  On a 150 x 150 grid (22,500 cells) it took 167 s and about 4,700 CPU-seconds, and needs about 4 GB; memory grows with the square of the number of cells.
  `lee.mc()` on the same grid with 99 permutations took 3 s.
  Neighbours: `spdep::cell2nb()` for adjacent cells, which numbers cells column by column from the bottom-left, unlike terra's row-by-row from the top-left, so values must be reordered to match; `spdep::dnearneigh()` for a distance band.
- **Agent model.**
  `lmerTest::lmer(dcum ~ agent + interval + (1 | lu))` for the main effects (`anova()` gives Type III F tests with Satterthwaite degrees of freedom), and a cell-means model `dcum ~ 0 + group + (1 | lu)`, where `group` is the observed agent x interval combination, for the comparisons; contrasts and joint F tests by `lmerTest::contest()`, adjusted with `stats::p.adjust(method = "holm")`.
  lmerTest `r pkg_ver("lmerTest")`, lme4 `r pkg_ver("lme4")`.
- **Disturbance agents.**
  In the pipeline these would come from the disturbance history the epoch back-cast already parses (most recent stand-replacing event per interval).
  Distance to the nearest disturbance is `terra::distance()`, once per agent.
- **Transitions.**
  `LandR::plotVegTransitions()` draws one `ggalluvial::geom_flow()` band per *pixel*, which is slow at district scale.
  Collapsing cells to their unique class paths first and weighting by area, as done here, gives the same plot from at most 4^7^ = 16,384 rows per zone.
  ggalluvial `r pkg_ver("ggalluvial")`.
- **Patch metrics** use landscapemetrics (`r pkg_ver("landscapemetrics")`), `landscapemetrics::calculate_lsm()` with the `lsm_c_*` functions listed in @tbl-metrics.
  It requires a projected raster with units in metres.
  Per-area metrics mask cells outside the area to `NA`.
- **Trends.**
  Theil-Sen slopes are the median of the 21 pairwise slopes per cell; Mann-Kendall p-values are from `stats::cor.test(method = "kendall", exact = TRUE)`, adjusted with `stats::p.adjust(method = "BH")`.
- **Packages.**
  spdep, landscapemetrics, ggalluvial, ggrepel, patchwork, lme4 and lmerTest are not yet in the project's `renv.lock`; this draft was rendered against a separate library.
  They would be added before any of this goes into the pipeline.
